newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong graft buster says can keep China graft out.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong graft buster says can keep China graft out.

text.p: Rampant corruption will not engulf freewheeling Hong Kong after the British colony reverts to Beijing's control in 1997, the territory's anti-graft boss predicted on Tuesday.

"There is no basis for such fears because we have a very good system of the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) working independently with a sound legal basis," ICAC chief Michael Leung told reporters during a business meeting.

"We have independent judiciary, we have Chinese cooperation to the full, so I don't see any need for pessimism in this area, because we can guarantee our operation in the Basic Law (Hong Kong's post-1997 constitution)," he said.
The bustling British-ruled territory of 6.3 million people reverts to China at midnight next June 30, ending more than 150 years of colonial rule.

Beijing has promised Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy as a Special Administrative Region of China, but jittery Hong Kong people have expressed fears that corruption will mimic China and grow unchecked in the capitalist outpost after the handover.
Corruption has spread rapidly in China as market reforms unfolded over the past two decades despite periodic crackdowns.
In a survey conducted last year by the ICAC, more than 70 percent of 1,100 respondents predicted the sovereignty transfer would fuel an upsurge in corruption in Hong Kong.
The survey also found 41 percent of respondents believed the anti-graft unit would be less effective due to interference from Chinese officials after the change of flag.
Leung reassured Hong Kong businessmen that neither he nor the ICAC would allow themselves to be influenced by Chinese or Hong Kong officials when pursuing any corruption case in the future.
"Nobody can stop me from doing this lawfully," he said. "The same will apply to the Chief Executive. He or she cannot stop me from pursuing a case under the law," Leung said.
"I have the full legal power to pursue a case without any interference from anybody, whether it is officials in Hong Kong or in China."
The graft-buster, who recently returned from Beijing after talks with the Chinese government, said China had promised its backing to keep graft out of Hong Kong after the handover.

"China has again pledged its strongest support to keep corruption free after 1997 and to let the ICAC continue to lead the fight against corruption," said Leung who met officials in Beijing and Guangdong province neighbouring Hong Kong last week.
But Leung urged the business community to come forward if the ICAC was to succeed in stemming corruption.
"Our future is only as good as the strength and support this community, including yourselves, give us," he said.
